title: Singing "Margie" and Sy Oliver writing the background
summary: After September 1937 rehearsals, Young sang "Margie" on the train and Sy Oliver wrote the arrangement around his vocal in D.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: But we went in that band together. I never forgot that. It was September, '37. And we rehearsed about two, three weeks in New York before we ever went out on a job with that band. And right after that we came right back and made "Margie, the record "Margie". "Annie Laurie" and "Margie" and some other things -- right after that. Right -- and I never
did do any singing in no band before. I never sang, you know, with Earl or anybody.

But one day I was singing that -- singing "Margie" on the train, and Sy heard it. Sy -- he said, wow. He said, why don't you sing that. I said, oh, I don't -- I never did any singing. He said, but that would be good. He said, sing that again for me. So, I sang it and he wrote down exactly how I was singing it. He had me sing it over and over the way I was singing it.

He said, you know what I'm going to do? He said, I'm going to write a background that fit the vocal -- behind the vocal. But he wrote the vocal first, and this is one of the few times anybody ever did that -- wrote the way a guy sang a song -- the vocal, and then made the background fit the vocal. That's why the reeds can answer it so good because he knew exactly what I was singing. And we did this on the train.

He got his pad out and his paper and right on the train one day. I never forgot that. We were going, I think, from Philadelphia to Washington. And he made -- he sketched it out on the train. So, he says, you know, you're singing in the key of D. You're singing -- I said, I don't sing. I told you I'm not a singer. I'm just fooling around with this things.
